objectives: Trace the surgical and immunologic milestones enabling successful organ transplantation.
Explain HLA matching, immunosuppression mechanisms, and brain-death criteria in organ allocation.
Evaluate emerging frontiers including xenotransplantation, ERAS protocols, and bioprinting.

slides.title: Foundations — vascular anastomosis, the first transplants, and the rejection barrier
slides.body:
Organ transplantation — moving a living organ from one body to another with functional survival — required solving two distinct problems: the **surgical problem** (how to reconnect blood vessels) and the **immunologic problem** (how to prevent the recipient's immune system from destroying the graft).

**Alexis Carrel** (1873-1944) solved the surgical problem. A French surgeon working first in Lyon and then at the Rockefeller Institute in New York, Carrel developed the **triangulation technique** for vascular anastomosis: placing three equidistant stay sutures around the vessel circumference to convert the circular lumen into a triangle, allowing precise continuous suturing of each side without back-wall entrapment. He also pioneered vessel preservation in cold saline and arterial patch grafting. Carrel received the **Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine in 1912** — the first Nobel awarded to an American-based researcher — specifically for his work on vascular suture and transplantation of organs. He successfully transplanted kidneys, hearts, and limbs in animals, achieving short-term function. The **Carrel patch** — a patch of donor aorta retained around the origin of renal arteries during kidney procurement — remains a standard technique in deceased-donor kidney transplantation.

Yet every animal organ transplant eventually failed: the immune system — then not fully understood — rejected the graft. The immunologic barrier dominated the first half of the twentieth century.

**Joseph E. Murray** (1919-2012) performed the first successful human organ transplant on **December 23, 1954**, at Peter Bent Brigham Hospital, Boston: a kidney transplanted between **Richard and Ronald Herrick**, identical twins. Because identical twins share the same HLA (human leukocyte antigen) genotype, no immunosuppression was required, and Richard Herrick survived 8 years with the transplanted kidney. Murray received the **Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine in 1990**, shared with **E. Donnall Thomas** (for bone marrow transplantation). Murray subsequently showed that whole-body irradiation could achieve sufficient immunosuppression for non-twin renal transplants — technically successful but carrying enormous toxicity.

**Christiaan Barnard** (1922-2001), a South African cardiac surgeon trained in part under **C. Walton Lillehei** at the University of Minnesota, performed the first human **heart transplant** on **December 3, 1967**, at Groote Schuur Hospital, Cape Town. The recipient, **Louis Washkansky**, survived 18 days, dying of pneumonia — immunosuppression was too high, leaving him vulnerable to infection. Barnard's technical feat electrified the world and initiated a wave of cardiac transplantation. However, early results were poor until immunosuppression was refined. **Norman Shumway** (Stanford University), who had developed the surgical technique of orthotopic cardiac transplantation with **Richard Lower** in animal models during the late 1950s, built the program that achieved durable long-term results. Shumway's group published the key studies establishing endomyocardial biopsy as the gold standard for rejection surveillance.

**Thomas E. Starzl** (1926-2017) at the University of Pittsburgh performed the first human **liver transplant** in 1963 (the patient died intra-operatively) and the first successful liver transplant with long-term survival in 1967. Starzl also pioneered **multi-organ transplantation** and the concept of **tolerance induction**. His 1963 paper in *Surgery, Gynecology & Obstetrics* laid the technical groundwork for hepatic transplantation, and his 1989 *New England Journal of Medicine* paper demonstrated the efficacy of **FK506 (tacrolimus)** as a rescue agent for refractory rejection.

slides.title: Immunosuppression — from azathioprine to tacrolimus and HLA matching
slides.body:
**Immunosuppression** — the pharmacologic suppression of the adaptive immune response to prevent graft rejection — is the keystone of all solid-organ transplantation. Its history runs in parallel with transplant surgery.

**Azathioprine** (developed as **6-mercaptopurine** by **Gertrude Elion** and **George Hitchings** at Burroughs Wellcome, who shared the **Nobel Prize in 1988** for this and related work) was the first effective immunosuppressant in clinical transplantation. **Roy Calne** at Cambridge (working with Murray) demonstrated in 1960 that azathioprine extended canine renal allograft survival; it became the foundation of early human transplant regimens combined with steroids.

**Ciclosporin (cyclosporine, CsA)**: the pivotal breakthrough. Discovered by **Jean Borel** at **Sandoz AG** (Basel, Switzerland) in **1976** in soil fungal metabolites (*Tolypocladium inflatum*) collected in Norway; Borel demonstrated its selective T-cell immunosuppressive activity without the bone marrow toxicity of azathioprine. **Roy Calne** (Cambridge) conducted the landmark clinical trials demonstrating ciclosporin's efficacy in renal transplantation, published in *Lancet* in 1978. Ciclosporin works by binding **cyclophilin** in T-cells, forming a complex that inhibits **calcineurin** — a phosphatase required to activate **NFAT (nuclear factor of activated T-cells)** and drive **IL-2 transcription**. Without IL-2, helper T-cells cannot proliferate and the adaptive rejection response is blunted. Ciclosporin transformed transplantation: one-year renal allograft survival improved from approximately 50% to over 80%.

**Tacrolimus (FK506)**, isolated from *Streptomyces tsukubaensis* by the **Fujisawa Pharmaceutical Company** (Japan) in 1984, has a similar mechanism to ciclosporin — it binds **FKBP12** instead of cyclophilin, but the resulting complex also inhibits calcineurin. Tacrolimus is approximately 100× more potent than ciclosporin and became the cornerstone of maintenance immunosuppression from the 1990s onward following **Starzl's 1989 landmark publication**. Side effects: nephrotoxicity (shared with ciclosporin), neurotoxicity, new-onset diabetes after transplant (NODAT).

**Mycophenolate mofetil (MMF)**: inhibits **inosine monophosphate dehydrogenase (IMPDH)**, selectively blocking de novo purine synthesis in lymphocytes (most cells can use the salvage pathway; lymphocytes cannot). Replaced azathioprine in most protocols in the late 1990s.

**mTOR inhibitors** (sirolimus/rapamycin, everolimus): bind FKBP12 but the complex inhibits **mTOR (mechanistic target of rapamycin)** rather than calcineurin, blocking T-cell cycle progression at G1-S. Used in renal-sparing protocols.

**HLA matching**: Human leukocyte antigens (encoded by the **Major Histocompatibility Complex — MHC — on chromosome 6**) are the primary targets of allograft rejection. Matching at HLA-A, -B, and -DR loci (the most clinically relevant in solid-organ transplantation) reduces rejection risk. Full 6-antigen match (zero-mismatch) in living donor renal transplantation confers the best long-term graft survival. In deceased-donor transplantation, the **UNOS (United Network for Organ Sharing)** allocation algorithm weighs HLA mismatch, waiting time, geographic proximity, sensitization (PRA — panel reactive antibody levels), and pediatric priority.

**Brain-death criteria** (the legal and medical basis for deceased-donor organ procurement) were established in the **1968 Harvard Criteria** (*JAMA*, 1968, Report of the Ad Hoc Committee of the Harvard Medical School) — defining irreversible coma (brain death) as the cessation of all brain functions including the brainstem. Clinical criteria include absence of: responsiveness, brainstem reflexes (pupillary, corneal, oculocephalic, oculovestibular, gag, cough), and apnea (PaCO₂ rises ≥ 20 mmHg above baseline without respiratory effort during apnea testing). Confirmatory tests include EEG (isoelectric), cerebral angiography (no intracranial flow), and nuclear brain perfusion scanning.

slides.title: ERAS, xenotransplantation, and the regenerative frontier
slides.body:
**ERAS (Enhanced Recovery After Surgery)**: a multimodal, evidence-based perioperative care pathway that optimizes every phase of a surgical patient's journey — preoperative, intra-operative, and postoperative — to accelerate physiologic recovery and shorten hospital stay.

**Henrik Kehlet** (Copenhagen, Denmark) pioneered ERAS beginning in the 1990s with his landmark studies on fast-track colonic surgery, demonstrating that a bundle of interventions — preoperative carbohydrate loading (preventing catabolic stress response), avoidance of bowel preparation, regional anesthesia (epidural), normothermia, goal-directed fluid therapy, early enteral feeding, early mobilization, and multimodal analgesia (minimizing opioids) — reduced length of stay for colorectal resection from 9-12 days to 2-3 days without increasing complications. Kehlet's foundational paper appeared in *Lancet* (1997) and catalyzed the international **ERAS Society** (founded 2010), which now publishes evidence-based protocols for over 20 surgical specialties. The **ERAS Society guidelines** for colorectal surgery (Gustafsson et al., *World Journal of Surgery*, 2019) represent the international standard.

**Xenotransplantation** — transplantation from a non-human species into humans — has been the aspiration for addressing the chronic shortage of donor organs (approximately 100,000 Americans on transplant waiting lists at any given time; 20 people die per day waiting).
- **Initial attempts**: Reemtsma et al. transplanted **chimpanzee kidneys** into humans in 1963-1964, with one patient surviving 9 months. Barnard transplanted a chimpanzee heart into a patient in 1977 (survival: 4 days).
- **The pig as donor**: Pigs are the preferred xenotransplant species because of size, physiology, and the ability to breed large numbers rapidly. The primary immunologic barrier is the **galactose-α-1,3-galactose (alpha-gal) epitope** on pig endothelium, which triggers **hyperacute rejection** (complement-mediated destruction within minutes) in humans and Old World primates, who have preformed anti-Gal antibodies.
- **Genetically modified pigs**: The knockout of the **GGTA1 gene** (encoding alpha-1,3-galactosyltransferase) eliminates the alpha-Gal epitope. Additional genetic modifications knock out other pig complement regulatory proteins and knock in human complement regulatory genes (CD46, CD55, CD59), HLA, and thromboregulatory molecules.
- **January 2022, University of Maryland**: Surgeons **Bartley Griffith** and **Muhammad Mohiuddin** transplanted the heart of a **10-gene-edited pig** (bred by **Revivicor**, a subsidiary of **United Therapeutics**) into **David Bennett Sr.**, the first living human to receive a genetically engineered pig heart. Bennett survived **60 days** — the longest survival of a xenotransplant heart in a human at that time — before dying of a combination of rejection, viral (porcine cytomegalovirus) infection, and the underlying severity of his cardiac disease.
- A second pig heart xenotransplant was performed at NYU Langone (2024) with improved outcomes as protocols evolved.

**Bioprinting and regenerative medicine**: the long-term goal is organ replacement without donor dependency.
- **Anthony Atala** (Wake Forest Institute for Regenerative Medicine) demonstrated implantation of **bioengineered bladders** (scaffold seeded with autologous cells) in patients with myelomeningocele in a 2006 *Lancet* paper — the first engineered solid organs implanted in humans.
- **3D bioprinting** (layered deposition of cell-laden bioinks) has produced vascularized cardiac patches (Dvir group, Tel Aviv, 2019, *Advanced Science*) and perfusable liver tissue segments in the laboratory.
- The fundamental unsolved challenge is **vascularization**: engineered tissue beyond ~200 μm thickness becomes necrotic without a blood supply. Establishing a capillary network within printed tissue — the **vascularization problem** — remains the central barrier to printing whole solid organs.
- **Decellularization-recellularization** (Harald Ott, Massachusetts General Hospital, *Nature Medicine*, 2008): a whole rat heart was decellularized to its extracellular matrix scaffold, then reseeded with neonatal cardiomyocytes; the construct showed spontaneous contraction — a proof-of-concept for whole-organ bioengineering.

question.question: Ciclosporin's immunosuppressive mechanism involves inhibiting which enzyme, thereby blocking IL-2 transcription and T-cell proliferation?
options: mTOR (mechanistic target of rapamycin), which controls T-cell entry into S-phase of the cell cycle.
IMPDH (inosine monophosphate dehydrogenase), which is required for de novo purine synthesis in lymphocytes.

Calcineurin, a serine-threonine phosphatase required to dephosphorylate NFAT (nuclear factor of activated T-cells). When calcineurin is active, it dephosphorylates NFAT, allowing NFAT to translocate into the nucleus and drive IL-2 gene transcription. IL-2 is the principal T-cell growth factor; without it, clonal expansion of antigen-specific T-cells is blocked and the rejection response is suppressed. Ciclosporin binds cyclophilin inside the T-cell; the ciclosporin-cyclophilin complex then binds and inhibits calcineurin. Tacrolimus (FK506) achieves the same outcome by binding FKBP12, forming a complex that also inhibits calcineurin — hence both are termed calcineurin inhibitors (CNIs). Jean Borel discovered ciclosporin's immunosuppressive activity at Sandoz in 1976; Roy Calne conducted the pivotal clinical trials in renal transplantation published in Lancet in 1978.
DNA polymerase, by incorporating as a false nucleoside analog and terminating DNA replication in dividing lymphocytes.
question.explanation: Ciclosporin and tacrolimus are both calcineurin inhibitors (CNIs). mTOR inhibition is the mechanism of sirolimus/rapamycin. IMPDH inhibition is the mechanism of mycophenolate mofetil. DNA polymerase inhibition describes antiviral agents such as acyclovir, not immunosuppressants.

hints: Think about the IL-2 pathway: what step is blocked between TCR activation and IL-2 transcription?
Ciclosporin binds cyclophilin; the complex then targets a phosphatase.
slides.workedSolution: TCR activation → calcineurin activation → dephosphorylation of NFAT → NFAT nuclear translocation → IL-2 transcription → T-cell proliferation. Ciclosporin (binding cyclophilin) and tacrolimus (binding FKBP12) both form complexes that inhibit calcineurin at the same step, blocking NFAT dephosphorylation and halting IL-2 production. The result is selective suppression of T-lymphocyte clonal expansion — the key effectors of acute cellular rejection.

question.question: A deceased donor's kidneys are offered to two candidates. Candidate A has 3 HLA mismatches; Candidate B has 1 HLA mismatch. If each additional HLA mismatch reduces estimated 10-year graft survival by 4 percentage points from a baseline of 72%, what is the estimated 10-year graft survival (%) for each candidate? Give the answer for Candidate A first, then Candidate B (format: 'A: X%, B: Y%').
Reason through the immunologic barriers that caused hyperacute rejection in early pig-to-human transplants and how genetic modification overcomes them.
question.goal: Explain the alpha-Gal epitope mechanism and how GGTA1 knockout and human transgene insertion address it.

steps.prompt: Why do humans have preformed antibodies against pig tissue before any prior pig organ exposure?

acceptedAnswers: humans are exposed to gut bacteria expressing alpha-Gal epitopes; this generates high-titer natural IgM and IgG anti-Gal antibodies that cross-react with the same epitope on pig endothelium

hints: Alpha-Gal is expressed on gut bacteria as well as pig cells.
These antibodies arise from normal immune exposure to commensal organisms.
steps.reveal: Humans (and Old World primates) lack the enzyme alpha-1,3-galactosyltransferase (GGTA1) and therefore do not express alpha-Gal on their own cells — but they are exposed throughout life to gut bacteria (E. coli, Salmonella, and others) that express alpha-Gal. This chronic exposure generates high-titer **natural (preformed) anti-Gal antibodies** (predominantly IgM, also IgG) without any deliberate immunization. When pig endothelium — which is richly coated with alpha-Gal — is exposed to human blood, preformed anti-Gal antibodies bind immediately, activate complement via the classical pathway, and destroy the graft vasculature within minutes: **hyperacute rejection**.

steps.prompt: How does knockout of the GGTA1 gene in pigs address this barrier?
steps.motivation: Mechanism of the primary genetic modification in xenotransplant pigs.

acceptedAnswers: without GGTA1, pig cells cannot synthesize the alpha-Gal epitope; preformed human anti-Gal antibodies have no target and hyperacute rejection is prevented

hints: GGTA1 encodes the enzyme that adds the alpha-Gal sugar to glycoproteins.
No enzyme → no sugar epitope → no antibody target.
steps.reveal: GGTA1 encodes alpha-1,3-galactosyltransferase — the enzyme that attaches the galactose-alpha-1,3-galactose disaccharide to cell surface glycoproteins. Knockout of GGTA1 (achieved by homologous recombination or CRISPR-Cas9 editing in pig embryos) eliminates the alpha-Gal epitope from all pig cells. The preformed human anti-Gal antibodies find no target on the graft endothelium, and the complement cascade is not activated — hyperacute rejection is prevented. The first GGTA1-knockout pigs were created in 2002 by **David Ayares** (Revivicor) and **Lai et al.** (*Science*, 2002).

steps.prompt: GGTA1 knockout eliminates hyperacute rejection, but acute humoral rejection (non-Gal antibody-mediated) persists. What additional genetic modifications in the 10-gene-edited pig used in the 2022 Maryland case address this?

acceptedAnswers: additional pig gene knockouts eliminate other pig antigens (Neu5Gc, beta-1,4-N-acetylgalactosaminyltransferase); human transgene insertions add complement regulatory proteins (CD46, CD55, CD59), thromboregulatory proteins (human thrombomodulin, endothelial protein C receptor), and HLA-E to reduce NK cell activity

hints: Beyond alpha-Gal, other pig carbohydrate antigens trigger human antibodies.
Human complement regulatory proteins on the pig endothelium prevent complement-mediated damage from the human side.
steps.reveal: The 10-gene-edited pig used by **Griffith and Mohiuddin** at Maryland in January 2022 carried: (1) three pig gene **knockouts** — GGTA1 (alpha-Gal), CMAH (synthesizes Neu5Gc, another xenoantigen), and B4GALNT2 (another carbohydrate antigen) — eliminating the three major pig carbohydrate antigens; and (2) seven human **transgene insertions** — CD46, CD55, CD59 (human complement regulatory proteins preventing complement-mediated graft injury), human thrombomodulin and endothelial protein C receptor (preventing thrombotic microangiopathy), HLA-E (reducing NK cell-mediated rejection), and CD47 (a 'don't eat me' signal preventing macrophage phagocytosis of pig cells). This multi-layer approach addressed sequential immunologic barriers, but porcine cytomegalovirus (pCMV) contamination — a pathogen missed in pre-implant screening — contributed to David Bennett's eventual decline.

question.prompt: In 180 words or fewer, explain why the kidney transplants performed by Joseph Murray in the 1950s did not require immunosuppression in the first successful case, why subsequent non-twin transplants required it, and which two Nobel Prizes are relevant to the immunosuppression story. Name at least four named individuals (beyond Murray) and their specific contributions.
question.rubric: Should state: Murray's first successful transplant (December 23, 1954, Peter Bent Brigham Hospital) was between identical twins Richard and Ronald Herrick — identical twins share the same HLA genotype, so the recipient's immune system recognized the graft as self and did not mount a rejection response. Subsequent non-twin transplants required immunosuppression because MHC/HLA mismatches trigger T-cell-mediated and antibody-mediated rejection. The two Nobel Prizes: (1) Gertrude Elion and George Hitchings (Nobel 1988) for developing azathioprine/6-mercaptopurine — the first clinical immunosuppressant; (2) Murray and Thomas (Nobel 1990) for transplantation. Additional name-drops required: Jean Borel (Sandoz) discovering ciclosporin (1976); Roy Calne (Cambridge) conducting clinical ciclosporin trials and earlier canine azathioprine work; Thomas Starzl demonstrating tacrolimus rescue in liver transplantation (1989 NEJM paper); Norman Shumway developing cardiac transplant technique and rejection surveillance at Stanford. Bonus: mention that ciclosporin and tacrolimus are both calcineurin inhibitors despite binding different immunophilins (cyclophilin vs FKBP12).
